metadata.description: Why correlation isn't causation matters in practice, told through a real kidney-stone study: keyhole surgery looks better overall, but open surgery wins for both small and large stones — because the hard cases went to surgery. Built with real SQL that actually runs.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude UI, ask shown answered. Exact required intro phrasing (PM).
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Supriya and this video is about why correlation isn't causation, and how real hospital data can point you to the wrong answer.

props.command: claude "which kidney stone treatment works better?"

beats.role_note: Manim — the stakes: a real choice between two treatments
beats.narration_text: Here's the problem. A study compared two ways of treating kidney stones: open surgery, and a keyhole procedure. Three hundred fifty patients each. The data is real, from a British Medical Journal study in nineteen eighty-six. Say you run the hospital. You have to pick one.
beats.visual_intent: Two labelled columns of 350 patient dots each fade in: 'Open surgery' and 'Keyhole (PCNL)'. A question card 'Which one do you pick?' settles between them. Source line beneath: 'Charig et al., BMJ 1986'. Corner handle 'Supriya'.

beats.narration_text: So the ask: compare the success rate of each treatment. Success means the stones were gone, or nearly gone, three months later.

props.command: claude "compare success rates for open surgery vs keyhole in kidney_stones"

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — cycle 1, the actual query (sql/q1_by_treatment.sql, verbatim)
beats.narration_text: Here's the query. One table, one row per treatment and stone size. Sum the successes, divide by the patients, group by treatment. Nothing fancy. Notice what it leaves out: which patients got which treatment.

props.title: q1_by_treatment.sql
props.code:
SELECT treatment,
       SUM(patients) AS patients,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(successes)
             / SUM(patients), 1)
         AS success_pct
FROM kidney_stones
GROUP BY treatment
ORDER BY success_pct DESC;

beats.role_note: Manim — cycle 1 output, the misleading answer (real sql/q1_by_treatment.out)
beats.narration_text: Keyhole: eighty-two point six percent. Open surgery: seventy-eight. Keyhole wins by almost five points. Most dashboards would stop right here.
beats.visual_intent: Two bars grow from zero: Keyhole (PCNL) 82.6%, Open surgery 78.0%; values count up to the real query output. A '+4.6 pts' bracket marks the gap; Keyhole bar gets the single terracotta accent. Corner handle 'Supriya'.

beats.narration_text: The revision. Large stones are harder to clear than small ones. So the change: split the same numbers by stone size.

props.command: claude "split the same comparison by stone size"

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — cycle 2, the revised query (sql/q2_by_size.sql, verbatim)
beats.narration_text: One change: stone size goes into the group by. Same table, same rows. I kept the patient count too, because it matters in a second.

props.title: q2_by_size.sql
props.code:
SELECT stone_size,
       treatment,
       SUM(patients) AS patients,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(successes)
             / SUM(patients), 1)
         AS success_pct
FROM kidney_stones
GROUP BY stone_size, treatment
ORDER BY stone_size DESC,
         success_pct DESC;

beats.role_note: Manim — cycle 2 output, the flip (real sql/q2_by_size.out)
beats.narration_text: Now look. Small stones: open surgery ninety-three percent, keyhole eighty-seven. Large stones: open surgery seventy-three, keyhole sixty-nine. Open surgery wins both groups.
beats.visual_intent: The two B04 bars split into two pairs: Small (<2 cm) — Open surgery 93.1% vs Keyhole 86.7%; Large (≥2 cm or multiple) — Open surgery 73.0% vs Keyhole 68.8%. The winning bar in each pair (surgery, both times) takes the terracotta accent. Corner handle 'Supriya'.

beats.role_note: Manim — why it flips: the patient mix (counts from sql/q2_by_size.out)
beats.narration_text: Here's why. Look at the patient counts. The hard cases went to surgery: two hundred sixty-three of its three hundred fifty patients had large stones. Keyhole got mostly easy ones: two hundred seventy small. Stone size drove the treatment and the outcome. The overall number measured the patients, not the procedure.
beats.visual_intent: The B01 dot columns re-sort by stone size (labels: 'small <2 cm', 'large ≥2 cm or multiple'): Open surgery 263 large / 87 small; Keyhole 80 large / 270 small, with counts labelled. An arrow labelled 'stone size' points to both 'treatment' and 'outcome'. Corner handle 'Supriya'.

beats.role_note: Manim — the lesson: three questions + the still-observational caveat
beats.narration_text: So the correlation was real. Keyhole patients did better. The gap came from the patient mix, not the procedure. Before you act on a gap, ask three things: who got which option, what else drives the outcome, and does the gap survive a split. And even the split is still observational. Only randomizing rules out the causes nobody measured.
beats.visual_intent: Three numbered questions build in one at a time, synced to narration: 'Who got which option?', 'What else drives the outcome?', 'Does the gap survive a split?'. Last, a quieter caveat line: 'A split is still observational — only randomizing rules out what nobody measured.' Corner handle 'Supriya'.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — 'Your turn.' prompt, read aloud and discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude with your own data: find a variable that drives both who got the treatment and the outcome, then re-run the comparison split by it. If the winner flips, your dashboard was measuring the mix, not the effect.

props.command: claude "find a variable driving both who got treated and the outcome; re-run split by it"

beats.role_note: title-restate outro — LAST beat. Full-size visible handle 'Supriya'.
beats.narration_text: Correlation Is Not Causation. Check who got what. I am Supriya.
